Essay:

One Activity Is Not Too Much

When I first heard that our principal wants every student to join at least one extracurricular activity, I was kind of mad. I already have homework and chores, and I have to watch my little brother on Thursdays. But then I thought about it more and I changed my mind. I agree with the principal, but only if the rule is flexible for kids who need it.

My first reason is that a lot of kids don't know what they like until somebody makes them try it. Last year my friend Marcus joined yearbook only because his mom made him. He complained about it for like two weeks. Then by October he was staying after school to fix the photo pages, and now he says he wants to do graphic design when he grows up. He never would of found that out if he just went home at 3:00 and played video games. Some kids are quiet or not sure of themselfs, and a rule like this gives them a push.

Another reason is that activities teach you stuff that classes don't. If I mess up in math, it only hurts my grade. But if I skip soccer practice, the whole team has to deal with it. Also kids on student council have to listen to people complain about the lunch food and then they have to actually plan things with real money. Adults have to do things like that all the time, and you can't learn it from a worksheet.

It also helps you meet people. Our school has around nine hundred kids, and you can go all three years only knowing the people in your classes. In a club there are kids from different grades and different friend groups. A sixth grader in chess club might play against an eighth grader, and then the hallway isn't so scary anymore. I think when kids feel like they belong somewhere they come to school more and get in less trouble.

I know some people will disagree with me. Some students have jobs or a really long bus ride, or they have to help their family, and some kids are just shy. Those are good points. That is why the rule should not be too strict. The school should have clubs that meet during lunch or advisory so nobody has to miss the bus. Small things should count too, like helping in the library once a week. And if a student really can't do anything, they should be able to talk to a counselor and get excused.

In conclusion, one activity is not that much to ask. It is only an hour or two a week, and you could get a new skill or a new friend out of it. Most of us would not sign up on our own, so I think the principal is right.
